newsitem.title: USA: US Dec spot natgas holds about $1 above Nov index.
newsitem.headline: US Dec spot natgas holds about $1 above Nov index.

text.p: U.S. spot natgas prices for Dec 1 delivery carried at least a $1 premium to November indices Friday, supported by cold weather forecasts and lower-than-normal storage levels ahead of winter, sources said.
December Gulf Coast prices were talked in the high-$3.90s early, but as the futures market slipped cash prices fell to about $3.80, still up about $1.10 from November index levels.
November gas on the Gulf Coast pipes was selling in the $3.60-3.80 area, with the softer-priced deals evident in late trading, sources said.
Forecasters call for below-normal temperatures next week through the Northeast and Midwest, with the coldest weather expected in the central and New England states.
The anticipated cold lifted New York city-gate prices for next month into the $5.05-5.25 range, almost $2 over November's index.
For weekend deliveries, gas at the city-gate sold mostly in the mid-$4 area.
In the Midcontinent, where historically-low storage levels are creating a panic among some buyers, December prices were talked in the $3.60s to low-$3.70s, up about $1.10 from Nov 1.
Forecasters call for temperatures about five to 10 degrees below-normal early next week throughout most of the Midwest.
Meanwhile, temperatures in Texas are expected to remain above-normal through the weekend, but cooler weather is forecast for next week.
December prices in south Texas were mostly in the mid-$3.60s to low-$3.70s, up more than a $1 from November indices.
In west Texas, Permian December prices hovered in the low-to-mid $3.60s, up nearly $1.50 from November 1.
Sources attributed the sharp rise in prices to low storage levels in the West and a strong western Canadian demand.
At the southern California border, the December market was in the $3.80s, up about $1.30 from December's index, traders said.
However, some traders are speculating the recent heavy rains and snow could put on a damper on the market in the near-term as hydroelectric power becomes more plentiful in the northwestern U.S.
